title: Judges 8:4–17
context: Judges 8:4–17 follows Gideon and the three hundred across the Jordan in pursuit of the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna. Exhausted, they ask for bread at Succoth and Penuel, two Israelite towns east of the Jordan, and are refused with taunts. Gideon threatens both towns, captures the kings at Karkor, and returns to carry out his threats: he punishes the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers, and breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills its men. The narrator records these acts without explicit comment, but the tone of the chapter shifts. Gideon now acts more on his own word than on the LORD’s, and the conflict with fellow Israelites contrasts sharply with his peacemaking in 8:1–3. The narrative invites readers to see here the beginning of the decline that marks the rest of his story.

verses.text: Gideon came to the Jordan and passed over, he and the three hundred men who were with him, faint, yet pursuing.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon and the three hundred cross the Jordan, “faint, yet pursuing.” Arminian readers note the perseverance of the small band, who press on despite exhaustion. Faithfulness in God’s work often means continuing when strength is low, and the phrase offers a fitting picture of persevering obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God sustains his servants through weariness, enabling them to finish the task he has given. The phrase captures human weakness and continued effort together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an image of perseverance, while recognizing that the narrative itself is about a military pursuit in Israel’s history.

verses.text: He said to the men of Succoth, “Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me; for they are faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks the men of Succoth for bread because his men “are faint.” The request is reasonable and courteous. Arminian readers note that Gideon is pursuing Israel’s enemies on behalf of all Israel, so the townspeople have a real obligation to help their kinsmen in need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a legitimate request from God’s appointed deliverer, made for the sake of those who follow him. Succoth is an Israelite town with a long history (compare Genesis 33:17). Shared ground: both traditions read the request as fair and as testing whether Succoth will stand with the LORD’s deliverance or hedge its bets.

verses.text: The princes of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?”
verses.arminianNotes: The princes of Succoth taunt, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?” Arminian readers note that the refusal reflects fear and self-interest. They will not commit until the outcome is certain, and so they withhold help from God’s people in need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Succoth’s refusal reveals unbelief: the town does not recognize God’s hand in the victory already won. Shared ground: both traditions read the response as a failure of solidarity and faith, and both note that the text presents it as a real wrong, even as the narrative goes on to raise questions about the severity of Gideon’s response.

verses.text: Gideon said, “Therefore when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, then I will tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon threatens to “tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers” once the LORD gives him the kings. Arminian readers note that Gideon still speaks of the LORD delivering the kings, but the threat itself is his own, not a command from God. The narrator does not record the LORD directing this response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the absence of any divine word authorizing the threat, in contrast with the LORD’s repeated instructions in chapter 7. Gideon’s anger now drives the action. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, recognizing that Scripture can record a leader’s actions without approving them, and both see a shift in Gideon’s character beginning here.

verses.text: He went up there to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way; and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon goes to Penuel and receives the same refusal. Arminian readers note that the repeated refusal shows a broader failure of solidarity among the Israelites east of the Jordan. Each town is responsible for its own choice, and both choose self-protection over support for God’s deliverer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Penuel, the place where Jacob met God face to face (Genesis 32:30), now refuses to help the LORD’s deliverer. The irony underscores the town’s spiritual failure. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confirming the pattern of 8:6 and preparing for Gideon’s return.

verses.text: He spoke also to the men of Penuel, saying, “When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon tells Penuel, “When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower.” Arminian readers note that Gideon’s confidence in returning “in peace” shows his trust that he will succeed. But the threat again comes from Gideon himself, without any recorded word from the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the tower likely represented the town’s security and strength, which it trusted instead of joining in the LORD’s deliverance. Gideon’s threat targets that misplaced confidence. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a sequence the narrator records without endorsing, and both read it in light of the tragic outcome in 8:17.

verses.text: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their armies with them, about fifteen thousand men, all who were left of all the army of the children of the east; for there fell one hundred twenty thousand men who drew sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebah and Zalmunna are at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that remain after “one hundred twenty thousand men who drew sword” have fallen. Arminian readers note the scale of the victory God has already given, and that Gideon still faces a substantial force with his three hundred.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the numbers as a reminder of how complete God’s deliverance had been, and how overwhelming the odds remain for the small band. Shared ground: both traditions read the figures as underlining the greatness of God’s work, and both acknowledge that interpreters differ on how such large numbers in ancient narrative should be understood.

verses.text: Gideon went up by the way of those who lived in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and struck the army; for the army felt secure.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon approaches by the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah and strikes the army, “for the army felt secure.” Arminian readers note that the enemy’s complacency proves its undoing. False security is a danger for anyone who assumes the threat has passed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God continuing to deliver Israel through Gideon, even as the narrative becomes more focused on Gideon’s own actions. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a further stage in the victory, and neither finds a doctrinal contrast in it.

verses.text: Zebah and Zalmunna fled and he pursued them. He took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and confused all the army.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebah and Zalmunna flee, but Gideon captures them and throws the army into confusion. Arminian readers note that Gideon’s perseverance from 8:4 is rewarded. The faint but persistent band completes the task by capturing the kings, ending the threat that had oppressed Israel for seven years (6:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the capture fulfills the confidence Gideon expressed in 8:7, and later Scripture treats the kings’ fall as God’s judgment: “all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna” (Psalm 83:11). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the pursuit and as God’s complete defeat of Midian’s leadership.

verses.text: Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle from the ascent of Heres.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon returns from battle by “the ascent of Heres.” Arminian readers note that this return sets up the reckoning with Succoth and Penuel. The narrative pauses briefly before Gideon carries out his threats, and the reader is left to wonder whether the victor will show the restraint he showed toward Ephraim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief transition shifts the focus from the external enemy to Gideon’s dealings with fellow Israelites. The story will now test how Gideon uses his victory. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple narrative transition, and neither finds a theological dispute in it.

verses.text: He caught a young man of the men of Succoth, and inquired of him; and he described for him the princes of Succoth, and its elders, seventy-seven men.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon catches a young man of Succoth, who describes the princes and elders, “seventy-seven men.” The Hebrew verb behind “described” is often rendered “wrote down.” Arminian readers note that Gideon targets the town’s leaders, those responsible for the refusal, rather than the whole town.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the precise count of seventy-seven leaders, which gives the account a concrete texture and shows that responsibility is being traced to particular people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for Gideon’s judgment on Succoth’s leaders, and both note the narrative’s focus on accountability for leaders.

verses.text: He came to the men of Succoth, and said, “See Zebah and Zalmunna, concerning whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are weary?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon confronts Succoth with the captured kings, quoting their taunt back to them. Arminian readers note that the town’s leaders are now confronted with the consequences of their choice. Their refusal was made in freedom, and they must face what came of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the taunt is repeated almost word for word, with “men who are weary” in place of “army,” stressing the cruelty of the refusal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as establishing Succoth’s guilt, while recognizing that the narrative goes on to raise questions about the measure of Gideon’s response.

verses.text: He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon takes the elders and “with them he taught the men of Succoth,” using thorns and briers as he had threatened. The WEB’s “taught” renders a Hebrew verb meaning to make someone know; some translations render the verse with a verb of threshing or punishing, in light of 8:7. Arminian readers note the harshness of the act and that it fulfills Gideon’s own threat rather than a command of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the narrator records the act without endorsing it, and that Gideon now acts as judge on his own initiative. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene soberly, acknowledging Succoth’s wrong but noting the narrative’s growing distance between Gideon’s actions and the LORD’s directions, a theme that culminates in 8:27.

verses.text: He broke down the tower of Penuel, and killed the men of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city. Arminian readers note that this goes beyond the threat recorded in 8:9, which mentioned only the tower. The violence against fellow Israelites is a troubling development, and the narrative leaves it without divine sanction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the episode as part of the narrative’s portrait of Gideon’s decline: the deliverer who once feared to act now kills his own countrymen. The text records the act without commending it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sobering reminder that God’s chosen instruments remain flawed, and both note the contrast with the humility of 8:1–3.
